ops._why: describe the example's code (the old notes described the Settings struct and constinit version)
paragraphs: A 12-factor Drogon service, from Example 01. Configuration comes from the environment (factor III): a small env() helper returns the variable or a default, so an unset variable never turns into a null pointer, and main() reads PG_CONNINFO, PG_POOL_SIZE and SERVICE_VERSION once at start-up.

/healthz answers while the process is up (liveness); /readyz runs SELECT 1 through the libpq pool and reports ready or down (readiness), so the probe that takes a Pod out of rotation is not the probe that restarts it. Handlers are lambdas with the request and callback types spelled out, which Drogon's handler binding needs.

Port binding (factor VII) is explicit in main(): the binary is self-contained, with no external web server in front of it. conan.lock pins every library, and the Containerfile builds with GCC 15 on UBI 10.

ops._why: notes follow the example's bulkhead
paragraphs: The bulkhead from Example 12: one TenantBulkhead per tenant, created on first use in a map guarded by a mutex. Each holds a lock-free std::atomic<int> with a capacity of five; try_acquire increments it with a compare-and-swap loop only while it is under capacity, so a full tenant is refused without blocking a Drogon worker.

A refused request gets 429 with "tenant capacity exceeded" at once: shed, don't queue, because a queue in front of a saturated tenant becomes the bottleneck. The example releases the slot after the order is stored; in production code an RAII guard makes the release exception-safe. One tenant's storm fills only its own five slots; other tenants keep their capacity.
Per-tenant connection pools at the libpq or gRPC layer are a separate bulkhead: the counter caps concurrency, the pool caps sockets.

ops._why: notes follow the example's write-back
paragraphs: Write-back from Example 25: PUT /write-back/metrics/{id} stores the payload in Redis under metric:<id>, adds the key to the writeback:dirty set and answers at cache speed. A background std::thread wakes every two seconds, reads the dirty set, upserts each metric into Postgres with INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO UPDATE, and removes the key from the set only after the upsert succeeds, so a failed write is retried on the next cycle.

The upsert makes a repeated flush harmless. The flusher has its own libpq connection, separate from the request handlers', and main() joins it after the shutdown flag is set (Appendix H). The risk is the one every write-back carries: a write that was acknowledged but not yet flushed is lost if Redis loses it, so keep write-back for data that tolerates that window, such as metrics.
